doc.title: Phil Mead interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, June 1, 2006

chapter: The Catatonic Five on the national stage
title: The 1956 European trip on Holland America ships
summary: They played passage on small student ships; Clifford Brown's death and the Andrea Doria sinking occurred that summer.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: Did you play on a boat?

The only job we had was going over then coming back on the Holland America lines. These were little ships. They’d been on the Indonesian line and they put them in this summer service for the students. These were small ships. We left on June 23, 1956, my 19th birthday that’s why I remember the date, on this little ship, and played ten days over. These were small, slow ships, just students. And you can imagine, it was a ten day house party and we’d play it over, and then we came back the first week in September on the Ziter cruise which was another Holland America line ship. Now two key things happened in the summer of ’56, you will remember one of them probably. Three days after we left

Clifford Brown was killed. He died on June 26, 1956 on the Pennsylvania Turnpike. Clifford was always my favorite musician, just technique, soul, whatever, just unbelievable. And we learned that on the ship. That was sad. The other thing that happened that summer was the Andrea Doria was sunk. And that’s fifty years ago exactly, 1956. And most people went back and forth to Europe on ships. Plane travel was very tough then. You really had to go up to Gander, Newfoundland and then over to Greenland and then over to Shannon. So people went by ship. But when a ship went down, holy mackerel, there were a whole bunch of people who didn’t have any way to get back from Europe to the United States because the ships were full, so they kind of squeezed some extra people in on our trip back in September because of that. We had a Texas oil millionaire on the ship with all these college kids, and he loved to play poker, and so the band would play and he would play poker with all of the students on the ship and he lost, in those days, some incredible amount of money, I don’t know, twenty thousand dollars, which to him wasn’t nothing, but a lot of kids got their tuition paid. And when he got off the ship he said “great music, it’s the best trip I ever had, the most fun I ever had.”
